title: The Cold Email Starter Pack Swap Sheet: 4 Beginner Habits and What to Use Instead
description: Swap "quick question", the calendar link, the 400-word email and "just bumping this" for what works. Before/after email and a 3-email sequence.
lead: This is the full starter pack swap sheet from the reel. "Quick question", a calendar link, 400 words and "just bumping this" are four small mistakes, not one big one. This guide shows what to swap each one for, why, and gives you a rewritten email and follow-up sequence to copy.
insider: We write every client campaign this way: short emails, one clear ask, and follow-ups that each add something new. For one agency client that brought in **2,146 interested replies out of 2,429 replies** in four and a half months. Fixing four habits once is easy. Writing, testing and improving them every day is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: Why it's four small mistakes

Most beginner cold emails don't fail because of one terrible line. They fail because of four habits that each cost a few replies: a lazy subject, a big ask, too many words and empty follow-ups. Fix all four and the gains add up.
The swap sheet

head: Starter pack habit
Why it hurts
Swap it for
rows: Subject: "quick question"
Everyone uses it, so it looks like every other cold email
Their first name, or a short subject about their problem
A calendar link
Asks a stranger to do work and give you 30 minutes
One specific time: "Thursday at 10am?"
400 words
Nobody reads a wall of text from a stranger on a phone
Under 75 words, one idea, one ask
"Just bumping this"
Adds nothing, so there's nothing new to reply to
Each follow-up adds something new

blocks.text: Swap 1: the subject line

In [Hunter's State of Cold Email report](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), based on **31 million emails** sent by Hunter users in 2025, subject lines with "quick question" got a **2.5% reply rate and 28.7% open rate**, vs **2.9% and 32.9%** for other subject lines. Hunter adds that this depends a lot on your industry, so treat it as a sign, not a law.
**What to use instead:** test the person's first name ("Sarah") against a short subject about their world ("new reps at Acme"). Hunter's data found 5 to 6 words was the sweet spot for subject lines.
Swap 2: the calendar link

A calendar link says "go find 30 minutes for me". That's a lot to ask from someone who has never heard of you. It also adds a link to your first email, and many senders keep the first email plain for deliverability. This is a common rule, not a study.
**What to use instead:** offer one time. "Thursday at 10am your time?" can be answered with one word. If the time doesn't work, they'll usually suggest another one, and that's still a reply.
Worth a quick chat Thursday at 10am your time?
Swap 3: the 400-word email

Short is a common rule for a reason: people read cold emails on their phone, between other things. Hunter's data is more mixed than most advice: emails of **61 to 80 words** got relatively high reply rates, but so did emails of **181 to 200 words**. Under 75 words is a safe starting point, not a magic number.
**What to use instead:** four short parts. A reason you're writing to them. The problem. One line of proof. One ask.
Before (the starter pack)

Subject: quick question. "Hi Sarah, I hope this email finds you well. My name is John and I'm the founder of XYZ Agency. We are a full-service growth agency that has helped companies across many industries..." (and 350 more words, then a calendar link)
After (under 75 words)

blocks.label: Rewritten email
blocks.text:
Subject: Sarah

Hi [first name],

Saw [company] is hiring two new sales reps. Congrats on the growth.

New reps usually need meetings on day one, not month three. We helped [similar company] book [real result] in [time].

Worth a quick chat Thursday at 10am your time?

[your name]
Fill the brackets with **real** details. Never invent a result. If you have no case study yet, offer something useful instead, like a short teardown of how they get leads today.
Swap 4: "just bumping this"

Follow-ups matter a lot. In the same [Hunter report](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), using **three messages instead of one increased total replies by 106% (6.8% vs 3.3%)**. But Hunter also found that people who followed up three or more times had a lower average reply rate. So: send about 3 emails, and make each one count.
"Just bumping this" gives the reader nothing new to reply to. Every follow-up should add one new thing: a new angle, a case study, or a soft close.
The 3-email sequence

blocks.label: Email 2: a new angle (3 days later)
blocks.text:
Hi [first name],

One more thought. Most [their role]s we talk to don't have a lead problem, they have a follow-up problem: [the pain in one line].

If that sounds familiar, happy to share how [similar company] fixed it. Worth a look?

[your name]

blocks.label: Email 2 option: a case study
blocks.text:
Hi [first name],

Quick example: [similar company] had the same [problem]. We [what you did, one line]. Result: [real number] in [time].

Want me to send the details?

[your name]

blocks.label: Email 3: the soft close (4 to 5 days later)
blocks.text:
Hi [first name],

I'll stop here so I don't crowd your inbox.

If [problem] becomes a priority later, just reply "later" and I'll check back next quarter.

[your name]
Worked example: what follow-ups add
Using Hunter's averages on a list of **1,000 people**:

items: Same list, same offer: **about 35 more replies** from two good follow-ups.

blocks.text: These are averages from Hunter's users. Your numbers depend on your list and your offer.
Common mistakes when you fix the starter pack

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: Cutting words but keeping "I hope this finds you well"
Cut the opener first. Start with them.
Offering one time with no time zone
Say "your time" so there's no confusion
Follow-ups that repeat email 1
Add one new thing each time: angle, proof or soft close
Sending 6 or 7 follow-ups
Stop around 3 emails, then move on or check back later
Inventing a case study to fill the bracket
Use real results only, or offer something free instead

blocks.text: Run your email through the swap sheet with Claude

blocks.label: Swap sheet prompt
blocks.text:
Here is my cold email and my follow-ups:
[paste them]

What I sell, in one sentence: [your offer]
Who I'm writing to: [role, industry]

Check them against these 4 rules and rewrite them:
1) Subject line: no "quick question". Give me 2 options: their first name, and a 3-6 word subject about their problem.
2) No calendar link. End with one specific time, like "Thursday at 10am your time?"
3) Email 1 under 75 words. Count the words and show the count.
4) Max 3 emails. Each follow-up adds one new thing: a new angle, a case study, or a soft close. No "just bumping this".
Use plain, simple English. Keep my facts. Don't invent results: leave [brackets] where I need to add real proof.

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: Each habit costs a few replies. Swap all four.

faq.a: No. In Hunter's data it did a bit worse on average, and Hunter says it depends on your industry. Test it against a first-name subject on your own list.

faq.q: When can I use a calendar link?
faq.a: After they say yes. Once someone replies "sure, let's talk", a calendar link saves both of you time.

faq.q: What if my offer needs more than 75 words to explain?
faq.a: The first email only needs to start a conversation, not explain everything. Save the details for when they reply.
A common rule is 2 to 4 days between emails. The bigger point is that each one adds something new.
